on_slide_text: Prelicensure RN · Management of Care · safety risk: high
slides.speaker_script: Safe Delegation and Supervision. The concept underneath it is care coordination, and the module rates its safety risk high — its top rating, so this is one to be able to do under pressure rather than one to recognise on a test. Here is the whole lesson in one sentence. Match the task to the delegatee, retain nursing judgment, communicate expectations, and evaluate the result. By the end you should be able to do three things: differentiate tasks that require nursing judgment from tasks that may be delegated; select an appropriate delegatee using patient stability, task predictability, and local scope; and provide direction, supervision, and outcome evaluation after delegation. We get there in three moves, and then spend the second half putting all of them against patient cues, because knowing this and doing it at the bedside are not the same skill.

slides.learning_objective: Enter the lesson through a single patient cue.
slides.speaker_script: We start with a cue rather than a definition, because that is the order the unit gives you: the patient arrives first and the explanation catches up later. Here it is. A newly admitted patient has changing neurologic findings. Decide now, before any of this is taught, what you would do and why that thing first. Write it somewhere you will still be able to read at the end, because this exact cue comes back as the first assessment item. Comparing the two answers is most of what the rest of this session is for.

card_data.presentation: A newly admitted patient has changing neurologic findings.
cues: Objective in play: Differentiate tasks that require nursing judgment from tasks that may be delegated.
card_data.prompt: Thirty seconds: what is your first action, and why that one first?

slides.speaker_script: Everything that follows answers one question. Match the task to the delegatee, retain nursing judgment, communicate expectations, and evaluate the result. Keep that sentence in view for the rest of the session. When a slide stops making sense it is almost always because you have lost which part of this sentence it is working on, and naming the part is the fastest way back. The lesson takes the question in three moves — decision frame, then communication, then supervision — and then asks you to apply all of them to cues you have not seen.

slides.learning_objective: Locate any cue on the map before acting on it.
slides.speaker_script: Map first, detail second. The lanes on the left are the lesson's teaching moves, in the order a nurse actually performs them; apply and evaluate on the right are where you are made to use them. The reason to show this before teaching any of it is orientation: every cue you meet today sits in one of these lanes, and knowing which lane a cue belongs to usually tells you what to do with it before you can explain why. When you get stuck later, come back to this slide rather than to the last one you read.

slides.slide_title: Warm-up: put the three moves in order
slides.learning_objective: Sequence the lesson's three moves before seeing them taught.
slides.speaker_script: One minute, before any of this is taught. These three headings are the whole lesson in order, but they are shuffled on the slide. Put them in the sequence the nurse actually performs them at the bedside, then compare with a neighbour before the reveal. Getting the order wrong here is more useful than getting it right: it shows you which move you would have skipped under pressure.

Assessment, teaching, evaluation, and unstable-patient decisions remain with the licensed nurse
slides.visual_notes: Section 1 of 3 from the source topic.
slides.speaker_script: Decision frame. The nurse assesses the patient and task before delegating. Assessment, teaching, evaluation, and unstable-patient decisions remain with the licensed nurse. This is the first of the three, and the two after it assume it. What you get wrong here does not stay here; it propagates quietly into every decision the rest of the lesson asks you to make. Do not move on until you can say this part back without the slide. The test is the objective: if you can differentiate tasks that require nursing judgment from tasks that may be delegated, this lane has done its job, and if you cannot, nothing later in the lesson will fix it — it will only hide it.

slides.speaker_script: Communication. State the task, expected result, reporting parameters, and time frame. Confirm understanding and availability for questions. This is the middle move, and it is where most of the disagreement in this lesson will sit: the point at which a defensible action and the priority action stop being the same answer. Do not move on until you can say this part back without the slide. The test is the objective: if you can select an appropriate delegatee using patient stability, task predictability, and local scope, this lane has done its job, and if you cannot, nothing later in the lesson will fix it — it will only hide it.

slides.visual_notes: Section 3 of 3 from the source topic.
slides.speaker_script: Supervision. Delegation transfers performance of a task, not accountability for the nursing decision. Reassess the patient and evaluate completion. This is the last of the three, and it is the one most often left implicit -- the step learners can describe accurately and then do not actually perform when the first two have gone well. Say it out loud; that is how it survives contact with a busy shift. Do not move on until you can say this part back without the slide. The test is the objective: if you can provide direction, supervision, and outcome evaluation after delegation, this lane has done its job, and if you cannot, nothing later in the lesson will fix it — it will only hide it.

slides.slide_title: Activity: match the cue to the move it calls for
slides.learning_objective: Match each cue to the lesson move that answers it.
slides.activity_prompt: Write the four matches and one sentence explaining one of them.
slides.speaker_script: Work in pairs, four minutes. Every cue on the left was written for one of the lesson moves on the right; your job is to say which, and to be able to defend one of the four out loud. Where the two of you match a cue differently, stop and stay there — you have found a cue whose lane is genuinely arguable, and those are worth more than the three you agreed on instantly. Bring one disagreement to the debrief.

left: A. A newly admitted patient has changing neurologic findings.
B. A stable patient needs routine intake and output recorded.
C. A patient requires initial teaching for a new diagnosis.
D. A delegatee reports a value outside the stated parameters.

slides.slide_title: Debrief: the reasoning behind each action
slides.learning_objective: Explain why each keyed action follows from its cue.
slides.speaker_script: Read these four rationales as a set rather than one at a time. They are deliberately repetitive: the same habit of mind is showing up behind four different cues, and that repetition is the teaching point rather than an accident of writing. A learner who memorises four rules will meet a fifth cue and stall. A learner who can name the one habit will handle cues this lesson never showed them. Say the habit out loud in your own words before you leave this slide.

slides.learning_objective: Choose the correct action for a single cue.
answer_key: C. Delegate measurement with clear reporting parameters and review the result.
slides.speaker_script: One question, and it targets the middle of the lesson. The cue is: A stable patient needs routine intake and output recorded. Read all four options and commit to one before the reveal, because the value of a checkpoint is in being wrong out loud rather than quietly. The reasoning you are being tested on is this: A predictable task may be delegated when direction and supervision are provided.

card_data.stem: A stable patient needs routine intake and output recorded. What should the nurse do?
options: A. Delay action until the end of the shift.
B. Document the finding without reassessment or follow-up.
C. Delegate measurement with clear reporting parameters and review the result.
D. Delegate the clinical judgment decision to unlicensed assistive personnel.
card_data.rationale: A predictable task may be delegated when direction and supervision are provided.

slides.learning_objective: Respond to a cue using the lesson's frame.
slides.activity_prompt: Two sentences: what you assess, then what you do.
answer_key: The registered nurse performs and evaluates the initial teaching.
Initial teaching and evaluation require nursing judgment.
slides.speaker_script: A bedside moment, and this time you write rather than choose. The situation: A patient requires initial teaching for a new diagnosis. Write two sentences before the debrief: one naming what you assess, one naming what you do about it. Keep them in that order, because the order is the judgement. The keyed reasoning is: Initial teaching and evaluation require nursing judgment.

card_data.presentation: A patient requires initial teaching for a new diagnosis.
cues: Keyed action: The registered nurse performs and evaluates the initial teaching.
Because: Initial teaching and evaluation require nursing judgment.
card_data.prompt: Write one assessment sentence and one action sentence.

slides.learning_objective: Sort cues by whether they require immediate action.
slides.activity_prompt: Place each cue and justify one.
answer_key: Act now: the cues whose keyed action is immediate
Act in sequence: the cues whose keyed action is verification or planning
slides.speaker_script: Two columns, and the sorting rule is the point of the slide. Put a cue on the left when delay changes the outcome for the patient, and on the right when the correct action is verification, planning or teaching that a short delay does not worsen. Justify one of your placements aloud. Learners who can sort these reliably are the ones who prioritise well under load.

slides.learning_objective: Record the lesson's decisions in a reusable frame.
slides.speaker_script: This is the lesson turned into something you can write down. The module asks you to be able to fill every one of these fields for any patient in this situation, and the value is in the blanks: a field you cannot complete is not a documentation gap, it is an assessment you have not done yet. Fill them now for the mini-case patient, and notice which field you reach for last — that one is your weak lane.

slides.slide_title: Capstone: choose the next safe action
slides.learning_objective: Select the priority action in the lesson's hardest cue.
answer_key: B. Assign the task to a competent team member or complete it as the nurse.
slides.speaker_script: The last question, and the hardest cue the topic carries: The task is permitted by policy but the delegatee has not demonstrated competence. All four options are things a nurse might plausibly do, which is what makes it a capstone rather than a checkpoint. Choose the priority action, not merely a defensible one. The reasoning that separates them: Permitted scope does not replace validation of individual competence.

card_data.scenario: The task is permitted by policy but the delegatee has not demonstrated competence.
card_data.stem: What is the priority nursing action?
options: A. Delay action until the end of the shift.
B. Assign the task to a competent team member or complete it as the nurse.
C. Document the finding without reassessment or follow-up.
D. Delegate the clinical judgment decision to unlicensed assistive personnel.
card_data.rationale: Permitted scope does not replace validation of individual competence.

slides.learning_objective: Retrieve the lesson's key points without notes.
on_slide_text: Provide direction, supervision, and outcome evaluation after delegation.
slides.speaker_script: Close the loop with no notes. Answer each of these aloud or on paper, one per lane of the lesson. The answers are on the slides you have just seen and in the facilitator guide, so this is retrieval rather than assessment. If any one of them produces silence across the room, that is the lane to re-teach before this cohort meets the situation on a real unit.

slides.learning_objective: Match the task to the delegatee, retain nursing judgment, communicate expectations, and evaluate the result.
slides.speaker_script: Close where we opened. The question was: Match the task to the delegatee, retain nursing judgment, communicate expectations, and evaluate the result. The lines on this slide are the module's own answer, and they are what should still be there in a week when the detail has gone. If you keep one, keep the first: Assess before delegating. Everything else here is that sentence applied to a different cue. Go back now to what you wrote at the opening case and see whether you would still do it.

defects.note: [generated] This package was assembled by lessons/build_from_topic.py from the SRC02 topic's own fields. No clinical content was added: every sentence in a script that makes a clinical claim is the module's own wording, interpolated verbatim. Speaker scripts are written to be said out loud, but the teaching frame around that wording is one generated voice applied to all seven topics, so the framing sentences recur across lessons and a teacher who runs more than one of them should vary them. lessons/nclex_sepsis_recognition/ is the hand-written comparison.

[clinical specificity] The source topic states its content qualitatively and names no numeric thresholds, scoring tools, drug names or timings. None were added. Programme-specific criteria and local policy must be supplied by the author.

[assessment] Distractors are the module's shared set, identical across every item and all implausible; used unchanged rather than invented. They should be replaced before the items are used for assessment rather than discussion. The keyed action and rationale are the module's.
[evidence] Slides are source-aligned to SRC02 (the author's own module), not source-grounded. No OpenStax text is reproduced.
[standards] No CA-BRN-ART3 standards_refs are proposed for generated packages; the author adds them per lesson if the package is offered as accreditation evidence.
